title: Bolstering Ecosystems Against Coastal Harm Act
official_summary:
Bolstering Ecosystems Against Coastal Harm Act or the BEACH Act

This act modifies the coastal areas belonging to the John H. Chafee Coastal Barrier Resources System (CBRS) and which are, therefore, ineligible to receive federal financial assistance for land development. It also expands exceptions to this restriction, establishes additional requirements for agencies administering the CBRS, and requires a study relating to coastal barrier ecosystems.

Specifically, the act updates and replaces existing CBRS maps with maps recommended by the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) in a 2022 report to Congress titled John H. Chafee Coastal Barrier Resources System Hurricane Sandy Remapping Project. Affected coastal areas are located in 13 states: Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Rhode Island, South Carolina, and Virginia.

In addition, the act creates new exceptions to the limitation on federal financial assistance for certain (1) aquaculture operations (e.g., shellfish production) and (2) U.S. Army Corps of Engineers coastal storm risk management projects. The act also provides that insurable structures (i.e., walled and roofed buildings) that are on the ground in areas added to the CBRS within one year of enactment remain eligible for federal financial assistance. 

The act directs FWS to issue regulations requiring owners or lessors of real property in communities affected by the CBRS to disclose this information to prospective buyers or lessees.

Additionally, the act provides that FWS shall develop and finalize guidance relating to the expenditure of federal funds in emergency situations that threaten life, land, and property immediately adjacent to a system unit. The act also generally requires agencies that are involved with the CBRS to revise or issue regulations or guidance as necessary within one year of enactment.

Finally, the act directs FWS and the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) to conduct a scientific evaluation of the dynamics of coastal barrier ecosystems. FWS and USGS must provide related recommendations for the CBRS to Congress.

summary.headline: Law updates federal coastal barrier maps in 13 states and adds exceptions to limits on federal money for building in those areas.
summary.what_it_does: The law replaces maps for the John H. Chafee Coastal Barrier Resources System with new maps the Fish and Wildlife Service recommended in 2022. Land inside this system generally cannot get federal financial help for development. The law adds exceptions for some aquaculture, like shellfish farming, and for certain Army Corps of Engineers coastal storm projects. It also requires property disclosure rules, emergency spending guidance, and a scientific study of coastal barrier ecosystems.

who_it_affects.group: Property owners in coastal areas of 13 East and Gulf Coast states
who_it_affects.how: Their land may be added to or removed from the system, which changes whether new development there can get federal financial help.

who_it_affects.group: Owners of existing buildings in newly added areas
who_it_affects.how: Walled and roofed buildings already standing in newly added areas within one year of enactment stay eligible for federal financial help.

who_it_affects.group: People buying or renting property in affected communities
who_it_affects.how: Sellers and landlords will have to tell them whether the property is affected by the system, under rules the Fish and Wildlife Service must write.

who_it_affects.group: Shellfish farmers and other aquaculture operations
who_it_affects.how: Certain operations become eligible for federal financial help even inside the system.

who_it_affects.group: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and coastal communities
who_it_affects.how: Certain Corps coastal storm risk projects can now use federal funds in system areas.

who_it_affects.group: Federal agencies involved with the system
who_it_affects.how: They must update or issue rules and guidance within one year, and the Fish and Wildlife Service and U.S. Geological Survey must study coastal barriers and report recommendations to Congress.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: Enacted November 25, 2024; agencies must revise or issue rules and guidance within one year.
